fields.description:
## Why
Writable container layers are each container's overlay2 `upperdir`. They grow independently of
image layers and build cache, no prune reaches them, and nothing measured them on 2026-09-02 —
the only signal was "root disk high". The last cap under ADR 0112.

## Mechanism decision, with evidence
The ticket offers a runtime storage quota "when compatible", else a reaper. **The quota is NOT
compatible here.** overlay2's `--storage-opt size=` (and the `overlay2.size` daemon default) is
accepted only when the filesystem backing `/var/lib/docker` is XFS mounted with `pquota`, else
the daemon refuses: `--storage-opt is supported only for overlay over xfs with 'pquota' mount
option`. That filesystem is ROOT here, and XFS reads quota options at MOUNT time and refuses
them on a remount — so it needs `rootflags=pquota` and a REBOOT: the constraint S4 (`2ba3`) hit
for `/var/tmp`, re-derived and binding here. Even after that reboot it is PER-CONTAINER, not an
aggregate ceiling, and applies at creation, so every live service must be recreated. So this
ships the mitigation, publishes which regime the box is in, and documents the enablement steps.

## What the reaper does NOT guarantee
1. **It cannot reclaim a RUNNING container's writable layer at all.** Only exited/dead ones are
   removable, so for the live compose set this is MEASUREMENT AND AN ALARM, not a bound; only
   the reboot-gated quota would bound those. Sharper than S4's fill rate, so it is said first.
2. For the debris it does bound, the bound is `cap + fill_rate x interval`: at 2 GiB and 300 s a
   sustained net fill above ~7.2 MB/s outruns it, and this gp3 volume does 125 MB/s (~17x).
3. Nothing that exited inside the 900 s grace window is removed, so a burst of fresh exits is
   unreclaimable by design. When it cannot get under the share it SAYS SO.

## Safety — proved against the live set
`docker container prune --filter until=…` cannot express what this host needs: its filters are
`until` and `label` only, with NO name filter. `autodeploy.sh` starts the mcp blue-green backends
with a bare `docker run` compose never sees, and reaps them in `mcp_retire_sweep` under a guard
this reaper cannot replicate — it reads the nginx `/mcp/` upstream include and refuses to reap
an exited container still named as the live backend, since `--restart always` would have
restored it. Reaping one anyway is bug `9ea3`: a transient exit became a permanent 502 on
2026-09-02. So candidates are enumerated and removed individually, sparing:

* anything labelled `com.docker.compose.project` (gerrit, review-bot, opcert, compose-mcp-1):
  an exited compose service is a crashed one whose logs are the evidence;
* anything labelled `rebar.service` (`mcp_run_new`'s stable identity);
* anything matching `^(rebar-mcp|compose-mcp-1)` — `mcp_managed`'s regex, so the two agree.

Two daemon-enforced guarantees, not shell logic: candidates come from `docker ps -a --filter
status=exited --filter status=dead`, which never lists a running container; removal is
`docker rm` WITHOUT `-f`, which the daemon refuses for a running one (the precedent
`mcp_retire_image` relies on). No `-v`/`--volumes`; `docker system prune` never used.

## What invokes the reaper, and what publishes the heartbeat
Two DIFFERENT callers; naming one is how a heartbeat ends up with no producer.
* The REAPER runs from its own `rebar-container-reaper.timer` (5 min, `TimeoutStartSec` nested
  strictly below the period per bug `1205`), rendered by `--print-units` and installed by
  `compose-up.sh` beside the three caps it already installs. A timer rather than a hook in the
  autodeploy tick, since `prune_docker_caches` runs only on deploy/backoff/pressure paths and a
  quiescent `main` never reaps.
* The HEARTBEAT comes from `observability.sh`, whose 5-minute timer already exists
  (`install-observability.sh`); §2i calls the side-effect-free `--check-active`. So "every tick"
  is the OBSERVABILITY tick, and the heartbeat still has a producer when the reaper timer is the
  dead thing — the point of having it.

## Observability (S2's publish-or-stay-silent rule)
§2i, from the SAME single `docker system df` call §2f already makes — the format string gains
`{{.Reclaimable}}` rather than a second daemon walk: `container_writable_bytes` (Containers
Size), `container_exited_bytes` (Containers Reclaimable), `container_writable_used_percent`
(`pct_of_cap`, S3's helper, reused), `container_reaper_active` (1/0 heartbeat) and
`container_quota_enforceable` (1/0: is the kernel enforcing XFS project quota on the Docker root
fs, i.e. could a ceiling exist at all). Non-heartbeat readings publish ONLY on success.

**Field surface verified — MATCH.** `docker system df --format` exposes `{{.Reclaimable}}`; on
the Containers row `Size` sums writable layers (`SizeRw`) and `Reclaimable` is the non-running
subset, i.e. the stopped-container debris. Checked against the CLI reference before the
format string was changed. An unrecognised row or a missing third field publishes NOTHING for
that reading, so a rendering change degrades to silence.

## Alarms (`monitoring_autodeploy.tf`)
`rebar-container-writable-usage-high` (>85%) and `rebar-container-reaper-not-active` (<1).
**The second pre-empts the S4 finding**: without it a silently-dead timer leaves usage nominal
while nothing enforces anything. Both `treat_missing_data = "breaching"`, both SNS-wired.
`container_quota_enforceable` gets NO alarm: its honest value is 0 until the reboot, and an
alarm that pages continuously is muted within a day.

## Which file owns what, and one budget
`docker-storage-cap.sh` owns the BUDGET; `container-cap.sh` owns only the reaper, the checks and
the rendering. ADR 0112 puts this share INSIDE the Docker budget, so `docker-storage-cap.sh`
gains `DOCKER_CONTAINER_WRITABLE_BYTES` (2 GiB) carved out of the existing 20 GiB: BuildKit
5 GiB + writable 2 GiB + images 13 GiB = 20 GiB, where images was 15 GiB. `container-cap.sh`
READS the share, so no second literal can drift. The 2 GiB is a starting point under ADR 0112
decision 6, labelled as one: no writable-layer figure was captured at the outage.

## Scope
In, enumerated: NEW `infra/scripts/container-cap.sh`; `docker-storage-cap.sh` (third share);
`observability.sh` (§2i + extended parse); `compose-up.sh` (installs the timer);
`infra/terraform/monitoring_autodeploy.tf`; `infra/runbooks/review-bot-ops.md`;
`tests/scripts/test_docker_storage_cap.py` (its `DOCKER_IMAGE_SHARE_BYTES` assertions move to
the three-way split); `tests/unit/test_alarm_actions_terraform.py`; two NEW test files.
Out: overlay2 deletion, the BuildKit cap (S2), journald (S3), `/var/tmp` (S4), gate scratch.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `--reap` removes an exited unowned container when the footprint exceeds the share, nothing
      under it, reaps oldest-first to an 80% low-water mark, and WARNs naming the running and
      protected bytes when it cannot get under. (`tests/scripts/test_container_cap.py`)
- [ ] `--reap` removes nothing for each of: a `running` row; a `com.docker.compose.project`
      label; a `rebar.service` label; a `rebar-mcp-*` / `compose-mcp-1` name; an exit inside the
      grace window; an unreadable share. Its argv never contains `-f`, `-v`, `--volumes`,
      `system prune` or `container prune`. A test pins the name pattern to `mcp_managed`'s.
- [ ] `observability.sh` publishes the three readings from a parseable Containers row and NONE
      when it is absent or unparseable; percent clamped to 100; both heartbeats publish every
      tick including their 0 path; all five dimensionless.
- [ ] `docker-storage-cap.sh --print-env` states the third share, the three sum to the budget
      (5+2+13=20 GiB), and an over-subscribed split is refused.
- [ ] Both alarms exist by name, `treat_missing_data = "breaching"`, SNS-wired, asserted in
      `tests/unit/test_alarm_actions_terraform.py`; `terraform fmt -check`/`validate` pass.

- [ ] The runbook documents diagnosis, remediation, the `rootflags=pquota` + reboot steps, and
      forbids manual overlay2 deletion.
- [ ] Portability: Docker APIs, systemd and local pytest only; no CI-provider trigger.
